paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled examples with unlabeled ones. In an open-set setting, some unlabeled examples belong to categories absent from the labeled collection. These unfamiliar categories can damage learning. A common response is to identify and remove them, but errors in that screening step can undermine the resulting training data.

This paper changes the learning problem itself. Its binary decomposition strategy converts the original task into several standard binary semi-supervised problems, avoiding the explicit outlier detection procedure. The resulting method, BDMatch, addresses two difficulties introduced by this transformation: uneven class proportions and compromises in the learned representations. It uses adaptive logit adjustment for the first and label-specific feature learning for the second.

Experiments across varied benchmarks report that BDMatch outperforms the compared approaches and support the effectiveness of binary decomposition. The contribution is a different way to handle unfamiliar unlabeled categories: reorganize the classification task while explicitly addressing the training difficulties that this reorganization creates.
icml-2024-binary-decomposition-a-problem.tldr: BDMatch tackles open-set semi-supervised learning by decomposing it into binary tasks instead of detecting and filtering unfamiliar examples.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into numerical representations that reveal graph structure. DeepWalk learns these representations from local information collected through random walks. Its empirical success is difficult to explain mathematically because learning involves a nonconvex optimization problem, whose solutions are harder to characterize than those of classical spectral approaches.

The paper establishes convergence properties for DeepWalk on graphs generated by the Stochastic Block Model. This model provides a simplified setting with an underlying cluster structure, making it possible to study whether the learned representation recovers the organization that generated the graph. The analysis concerns DeepWalk's output, connecting its optimization procedure to a meaningful structural result.

The authors prove that even a one-dimensional embedding can recover the cluster structure with high probability in the studied setting. These guarantees parallel existing results for spectral embeddings on block models. Their significance is theoretical: a method supported by empirical evidence also receives a cluster-recovery guarantee under this specific graph model.
icml-2024-convergence-guarantees-for-the.tldr: The paper proves that DeepWalk can recover cluster structure with high probability, even in one dimension, on Stochastic Block Model graphs.

paragraphs: General-purpose vision models aim to support many visual tasks, including tasks outside their training domain. One approach learns from sequences of visual data without linguistic inputs. The paper identifies a practical obstacle for this direction: existing efforts can depend on very large models and enormous collections of visual training tokens.

The authors develop an autoregressive vision model designed to work with a limited dataset. Sequential autoregression supplies the organizing learning approach, while efficiency in model size and training data is a central design goal. The paper examines whether this more economical model can still handle a range of visual tasks when tested.

The empirical findings report proficiency across tasks involving both high-level and low-level semantic understanding, together with adaptability across tasks. They also report substantial reductions in parameter requirements and training data needs. This supports the possibility of developing generalist visual capabilities with a smaller resource footprint, making the approach relevant to efforts seeking more accessible vision-model training.
icml-2024-data-efficient-large-vision-mo.tldr: An autoregressive vision model demonstrates broad visual capabilities with substantially reduced model size and training data requirements.

paragraphs: A room impulse response describes how sound travels from a source to a receiver inside a room. Estimating it is difficult because sound reflects, diffracts, and is absorbed along its path. DeepNeRAP learns a continuous representation of a room's acoustics so it can infer responses for source and receiver positions absent from training.

The training process uses two cooperating acoustic agents: one emits sound and the other records it at different locations. Their observations provide a self-supervised signal for inferring the room's acoustic properties. This avoids requiring direct ground-truth impulse responses, which the abstract identifies as a requirement of many earlier approaches.

The learned field is grounded in physical principles, including reciprocity and globality, giving its representation an acoustic interpretation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report better impulse-response estimates than closely related methods. The practical contribution is a way to learn room-specific sound propagation from active acoustic observations and then extend those estimates to previously unobserved position pairs.
icml-2024-deep-neural-room-acoustics-pri.tldr: DeepNeRAP learns room acoustics from cooperating sound-emitting and sound-receiving agents without requiring ground-truth impulse responses.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains one optimization problem inside another. Distributing this work across machines can create heavy communication costs because workers repeatedly send full-dimensional gradient information to a server. Compressing these messages is attractive, but the nested problem structure makes bias in the estimated hypergradient a central difficulty.

The paper introduces a family of distributed bilevel algorithms with communication compression. Its initial method, C-SOBA, uses unbiased compression and has a convergence guarantee with linear speedup. That result depends on strong bounded-gradient assumptions. The authors then incorporate moving averages, error feedback, and repeated compression steps to develop additional algorithms with weaker assumptions and improved convergence properties.

Numerical experiments report a tenfold reduction in communication overhead without severe performance degradation. The work therefore addresses both the transmission burden and the mathematical consequences of compression. Its sequence of algorithms also distinguishes the simple initial construction from later variants designed to reduce its dependence on restrictive gradient assumptions.
icml-2024-distributed-bilevel-optimizati.tldr: Compressed distributed bilevel algorithms reduce communication overhead tenfold in experiments while providing convergence guarantees under differing assumptions.

paragraphs: A model may perform poorly when its test data differ from its training data. This paper approaches that distribution shift through data acquisition: given a limited budget and several possible source domains, how should training examples be collected to improve performance on a particular target domain?

The proposed Domain-wise Active Acquisition framework uses unlabeled data from the target test domain to guide collection. It updates the acquisition strategy iteratively as training examples accumulate. This makes the choice of where to obtain data responsive to the growing training collection and to information about the target distribution, rather than treating acquisition as a single fixed decision.

The authors provide theoretical support for effective approximation of the test distribution and report advantages in extensive real-world experiments. Their empirical evidence also indicates that improving acquisition can substantially improve performance under distribution shift. The contribution is a data-centered way to spend a constrained collection budget, with access to unlabeled target-domain data playing an explicit role.
icml-2024-domain-wise-data-acquisition-t.tldr: Domain-wise Active Acquisition uses unlabeled target data to iteratively guide a limited training-data budget across source domains.

paragraphs: Pretraining neural operators could improve learning when data for a particular partial differential equation task are scarce. However, PDE datasets vary substantially: they can contain long trajectories, multiple scales, and different dimensionalities. This diversity makes it difficult to build a shared pretrained model that transfers effectively across problems.

DPOT combines an autoregressive denoising pretraining strategy with a scalable architecture based on Fourier attention. The training strategy is intended to make pretraining more stable and efficient, while the architecture supports increasing model scale. The authors train models with up to half a billion parameters using more than ten PDE datasets containing over one hundred thousand trajectories.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results on the evaluated benchmarks and strong transfer to varied downstream PDE tasks, including three-dimensional data. These findings support the usefulness of combining diverse PDE pretraining with an architecture designed for scale. The resulting model is presented as a shared foundation for improving performance across downstream scientific modeling tasks.
icml-2024-dpot-auto-regressive-denoising.tldr: DPOT combines autoregressive denoising and Fourier attention to pretrain scalable PDE models that transfer effectively across downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Estimating the permanent of a nonnegative matrix is a difficult computational problem with applications across several fields. Sequential importance sampling is empirically very efficient for this task, but its accuracy is hard to guarantee because the variability of its sampling weights can be difficult to bound. Practical methods with accuracy guarantees have instead relied on rejection sampling.

The paper combines ideas from these two approaches. It constructs a sequential importance sampling variant whose sampling probabilities are proportional to the upper bound used by a corresponding rejection sampler. This makes that bound part of how samples are selected, bringing a tool associated with rejection sampling into the sequential estimation procedure.

The authors prove that their method is more efficient than its rejection sampling counterpart, with particular benefits when high accuracy is required. For permanent estimation, experiments show speedups reaching two orders of magnitude over a state-of-the-art rejection sampling method. The contribution connects practical sampling efficiency with the structure used to support reliable estimation.
icml-2024-estimating-the-permanent-by-ne.tldr: A sequential importance sampler built from rejection-sampling bounds provably improves efficiency and achieves up to hundredfold empirical speedups for permanent estimation.

paragraphs: Standard dot-product self-attention is widely used, but understanding how input changes affect its output presents a mathematical challenge. It is not globally Lipschitz, so a single global bound cannot control its sensitivity in the usual way. This complicates attempts to certify the robustness of models that contain it.

The paper develops Local Fine-grained Attention Sensitivity, or LoFAST, to analyze behavior around an unperturbed input. It quantifies how changes measured in the l2 norm affect attention outputs. The analysis shows that local sensitivity can be controlled through quantities associated with the attention weight matrices and the original input, allowing the bound to reflect the particular setting being examined.

The authors use this analysis to compute non-vacuous certified l2 robustness results for vision transformers on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. These certificates provide meaningful guarantees in the evaluated settings. The central insight is that the absence of global Lipschitz control still leaves room for useful, mathematically grounded local robustness analysis.
icml-2024-fine-grained-local-sensitivity.tldr: LoFAST bounds the local sensitivity of dot-product attention and enables meaningful certified robustness results for vision transformers.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks requires memory for optimization states as well as model parameters. Low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, reduces that burden by training fewer parameters. Its restriction of overall weight updates to low-rank matrices can also limit model performance, creating a tension between training memory and the flexibility of the updates.

The authors analyze LoRA's learning dynamics and find that they can be approximated by a random projection. This interpretation suggests a way to keep updates compact without permanently confining their overall effect to low rank. Their method, Flora, resamples projection matrices so that it can achieve high-rank updates while keeping optimization-state space complexity sublinear.

Experiments across different tasks and model architectures support the effectiveness of this approach. The conceptual contribution is to view low-rank adaptation through the lens of gradient compression. That perspective motivates changing the projections over time, preserving the memory advantage of compact optimization states while allowing a more flexible accumulated change to the model.
icml-2024-flora-low-rank-adapters-are-se.tldr: Flora resamples gradient projections to enable high-rank model updates while retaining sublinear memory use for optimization states.

paragraphs: This paper studies language-model agents through a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework. An LLM Planner produces language-based subgoals, while an Actor handles their low-level execution. The planner operates in a partially observable environment, so its decisions must account for incomplete information about the underlying state.

Under suitable assumptions about pretraining data, the authors prove that the planner performs Bayesian aggregated imitation learning through in-context learning. They also show that simply executing its proposed subgoals leads to linear regret in their framework. This establishes a theoretical reason to explore beyond the behavior suggested by the pretrained planner.

The proposed remedy adds epsilon-greedy exploration to the imitation-learning procedure. When pretraining error is small, the resulting method has sublinear regret, meaning its accumulated decision shortfall grows more slowly than the number of rounds. The framework also extends to planners that infer environmental transitions as world models and to coordination among multiple Actors. These are conditional theoretical results about the specified agent model.
icml-2024-from-words-to-actions-unveilin.tldr: A theoretical framework explains LLM planning as conditional Bayesian imitation learning and shows how exploration can yield sublinear regret.

paragraphs: Language models can revise reasoning, but deciding when revision is needed and where an error begins remains difficult without external feedback. GLoRe addresses this diagnosis problem with Stepwise Outcome Reward Models, or SORMs. These models use synthetic training data to approximate the expected future reward of an optimal policy.

The experiments find that SORMs locate incorrect reasoning steps more accurately than outcome reward models. This feedback supports two kinds of correction: a global refiner receives a question and draft answer, while a local refiner also receives a critique identifying the first reasoning error. Both refiners use synthetic training examples generated by reusing the data employed for SORM training.

Combining global and local corrections with an outcome reward model for reranking significantly outperforms either correction method alone and a best-of-three sampling baseline. On GSM8K, this strategy raises greedy-sampling accuracy for an already reinforcement-learning-finetuned LLaMA-2 13B model from 53% to 65%. The finding supports pairing error localization with complementary revision strategies.
icml-2024-glore-when-where-and-how-to-im.tldr: GLoRe combines step-level error feedback, global revision, and local correction to improve language-model reasoning accuracy.

paragraphs: Latent representations are often used for visualization, interpolation, and extracting useful features. In an equivariant model, these representations respond systematically to transformations of the input. The paper shows that ignoring this built-in structure when analyzing representations can reduce performance on downstream tasks.

The authors propose principles for projecting equivariant representations into invariant ones, which remove dependence on the relevant transformations. They examine two settings. For a permutation-equivariant variational autoencoder generating molecular graphs, they design a projection that preserves information without loss. For rotation-equivariant image representations, they find that random invariant projections retain a high degree of information.

In both examples, analyzing the invariant representations works better than analyzing their equivariant counterparts. The paper also illustrates related behavior in standard neural networks whose training encourages invariance through data augmentation. The implication is that a useful representation depends on how it is read: accounting for a model's transformation structure can improve what downstream analysis extracts from its latent space.
icml-2024-interpreting-equivariant-repre.tldr: Invariant projections improve the analysis of equivariant latent representations in molecular generation and image classification examples.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation updates a model through two adapter matrices, conventionally called A and B. This paper argues that using the same learning rate for both matrices in ADAM leads to suboptimal finetuning in networks with large width. The issue concerns how the two factors learn together during adaptation.

Using scaling arguments for wide networks, the authors show that equal learning rates do not support efficient feature learning. Their proposed correction, LoRA+, gives the two adapter matrices different learning rates with a carefully chosen fixed ratio. This is a change to the optimization setup that preserves the computational cost of the original LoRA method.

Across extensive experiments, LoRA+ reports finetuning speedups of up to roughly twofold and performance improvements of 1% to 2%. These results support the practical value of the theoretical analysis: even when the adapter structure stays the same, coordinating its two learning rates differently can improve both the speed and quality of adaptation.
icml-2024-lora-efficient-low-rank-adapta.tldr: LoRA+ assigns different learning rates to its two adapter matrices, improving finetuning speed and performance at the same computational cost.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching requires choosing matches while future opportunities remain uncertain. Such decisions arise in settings including advertising, ridesharing, crowdsourcing, and kidney exchange. An optimal decision accounts for an action's value-to-go: the expected final matching weight if that action is followed by optimal future choices. Computing this quantity is combinatorially complex.

MAGNOLIA trains a graph neural network to estimate value-to-go and thereby emulate the optimal online algorithm. The learned estimate connects a present matching decision to its expected consequences for the completed matching. Empirically, the approach produces high-weight matchings across a variety of tasks.

The paper also identifies a family of graph distributions common in spatial crowdsourcing for which local neighborhood information can efficiently approximate value-to-go. This provides a theoretical connection to graph neural networks, whose information aggregation is local. The justification applies to the identified distribution family, explaining why the architecture is particularly well suited to those matching problems.
icml-2024-magnolia-matching-algorithms-v.tldr: MAGNOLIA uses a graph neural network to estimate the future value of online matching decisions, with theoretical support for spatial graph distributions.

paragraphs: Machine learning models frequently descend from other models through finetuning, quantization, or distillation. These related models may share structure or parameter values, but managing them as an expanding collection creates storage and maintenance problems. Bugs may also pass between relatives, making it difficult to trace errors back to their origin.

MGit organizes this ecosystem with a lineage graph that records relationships among models. It combines that graph with parameter-storage optimizations and abstractions for testing, updating, and collaboration. Recording derivation relationships provides a common structure for managing the collection, while shared model properties create opportunities to reduce its storage footprint.

The evaluation reports storage reductions of up to sevenfold. In a user study involving twenty machine learning practitioners, participants completed a model-updating task three times faster on average with MGit. These findings show benefits in both resource use and a concrete maintenance workflow, supporting model lineage as a useful foundation for managing related models.
icml-2024-mgit-a-model-versioning-and-ma.tldr: MGit tracks model lineage to streamline storage and maintenance, reporting up to sevenfold storage savings and faster model updates.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes a research direction connecting machine learning with C*-algebra. The authors present C*-algebras as a natural generalization of complex numbers and argue that this mathematical setting offers a way to bring existing learning strategies together while accommodating more diverse and information-rich data models.

The paper explains the motivation for using this framework and discusses how to build learning models within it. Kernel methods and neural networks provide the two concrete contexts for its technical design considerations. The focus is on how the underlying mathematical language can shape model construction and connect learning approaches through a shared framework.

The authors also discuss open questions, challenges, and possible future applications. Its contribution is a proposed research agenda and an account of the considerations involved in pursuing it. The claimed opportunity is broader mathematical expressiveness and unification; the paper frames the development of C*-algebraic machine learning as an ongoing direction for investigation.
icml-2024-position-c-algebraic-machine-l.tldr: This position paper proposes C*-algebras as a mathematical framework for unifying learning methods and representing richer data.

paragraphs: The paper studies online optimization with exp-concave objectives when feedback consists of function values rather than directly supplied derivatives. Decisions are made over successive rounds, and performance is measured by regret, which captures accumulated shortfall. The central question is whether quantum methods can offer an advantage in this particular limited-feedback setting.

The authors propose quantum online quasi-Newton methods. Their approach uses a quantum-estimated, inexact gradient to approximate the Hessian, the quantity describing curvature of the objective. This allows the method to incorporate curvature information even though the problem supplies only zeroth-order feedback.

The stated guarantee is O(n log T) regret with O(1) queries per round, where n is the decision-space dimension and T is the number of rounds. The authors report an improvement by a factor of T to the two-thirds power over the optimal classical algorithm. The contribution is a theoretical quantum advantage for the specified online exp-concave problem, combining logarithmic dependence on the horizon with constant per-round query complexity.
icml-2024-quantum-algorithm-for-online-e.tldr: Quantum quasi-Newton methods achieve O(n log T) regret with constant queries per round for online exp-concave optimization with zeroth-order feedback.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can produce effective decisions in offline reinforcement learning, but their random sampling can also yield unstable performance. Without a confidence measure, it is difficult to assess how reliable a sampled decision is. ReDiffuser introduces such a measure and uses it as part of the decision-making procedure.

The method learns a confidence function based on Random Network Distillation. This function assigns a quantitative reliability assessment to sampled decisions, providing a signal for recognizing those considered dependable. The authors then integrate that signal into task-specific sampling procedures, connecting confidence estimation directly to how plans are generated.

The resulting procedures support adaptive-horizon planning and value-embedded planning. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on standard offline reinforcement learning datasets. The contribution is therefore both an assessment mechanism and a way to use that assessment during planning. The empirical findings support this combined design as a means of improving decisions produced by diffusion-based offline reinforcement learning.
icml-2024-rediffuser-reliable-decision-m.tldr: ReDiffuser integrates learned confidence estimates into diffusion-based planning and reports state-of-the-art offline reinforcement learning performance.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems permit only evaluations of an objective function and constrain solutions to a Riemannian manifold. Algorithms designed for ordinary Euclidean space do not automatically accommodate this geometry. The paper develops an accelerated zeroth-order method to address slow convergence and instability in this setting.

For an epsilon-approximate first-order stationary point, the method requires O(epsilon^(-7/4) d) function queries. Adding a small perturbation gives a second-order stationary-point guarantee with high probability at the same stated order up to logarithmic factors, matching a state-of-the-art Euclidean result. The authors also establish almost-sure asymptotic convergence through the Stable Manifold Theorem.

The robustness analysis permits larger smoothing parameters, with a stated scale of approximately epsilon^(7/8) d^(-1/2), up to logarithmic factors. This improves the existing result by the factor reported in the abstract. Together, the results extend strong query-efficiency guarantees to manifold-constrained optimization while strengthening the smoothing behavior associated with robustness. The conclusions concern stationary points and distinguish finite-query probabilistic guarantees from asymptotic convergence.
icml-2024-riemannian-accelerated-zeroth-.tldr: An accelerated derivative-free manifold optimizer improves query complexity and smoothing robustness, with first- and second-order stationarity guarantees.

paragraphs: Human writing and language-model output can both exhibit complex and varied behavior, making automated detection difficult. Binoculars approaches the task by contrasting two closely related pretrained language models. The authors find that a score derived from this comparison separates human and machine text accurately in their evaluations.

The detector needs only simple calculations using the two models and requires no detector training data. It can also detect output from multiple modern language models without modifications tailored to each generating model. This makes the comparison score the central mechanism for transferring detection across different sources of generated text.

Across a wide range of document types, the reported detector identifies more than 90% of generated samples from ChatGPT and other models at a false-positive rate of 0.01%. It achieves this without training on ChatGPT data. These empirical results support the usefulness of paired-model comparison for accurate zero-shot detection across the text sources and situations examined.
icml-2024-spotting-llms-with-binoculars-.tldr: Binoculars compares two pretrained language models to detect generated text accurately without detector training data or generator-specific modifications.

paragraphs: Counting neurons alone may hide another resource used by a neural network: the precision needed to represent its weights. This paper analyzes how weight precision, neuron count, and the preprocessing time required to construct a ReLU network interact. Its results distinguish representational possibilities from the cost of producing and describing those representations.

An exponential-time preprocessing construction demonstrates that greater weight precision can buy an exponential reduction in neuron count when computing high-complexity functions with Boolean input encoding. The authors then introduce a network-size measure that includes both neurons and weight precision. Under this accounting, exchanging neurons for precision generally cannot preserve the same total size.

The final result concerns construction time. With polynomial-time preprocessing, arbitrarily high weight precision alone cannot deliver a nontrivial reduction in neuron count in the studied framework. Together, the results show why a compact neuron count can be misleading: the apparent saving may depend on expensive weight descriptions and an expensive procedure for constructing the network.
icml-2024-the-effect-of-weight-precision.tldr: Higher weight precision can reduce ReLU neuron counts through expensive preprocessing, but the savings change when precision and construction time are counted.

paragraphs: Positional encoding tells a language model where elements occur in a sequence. This paper uses the observation that language sequences have an intrinsic segmentation structure. Its Bilevel Positional Encoding, or BiPE, separates positional information into locations inside segments and relationships across segments.

For each position, BiPE combines two encodings. An absolute intra-segment encoding identifies the location within a segment and helps capture its semantic content. A relative inter-segment encoding represents the segment index and relationships between segments, with the aim of improving extrapolation to longer sequences. This gives the two levels of sequence organization distinct representational roles.

The theoretical analysis finds that separating positional information in this way makes learning more effective. Empirical results also report superior length extrapolation across a broad range of tasks and text modalities. The contribution is a positional design that uses language's segmented organization to support both local semantic learning and relationships across a longer sequence.
icml-2024-two-stones-hit-one-bird-bileve.tldr: BiPE combines absolute positions within segments and relative positions between segments to improve language-model length extrapolation.

paragraphs: MLP-Mixer architectures have performed well empirically, but their advantage over conventional multilayer perceptrons has been less clearly understood. This paper identifies sparsity as a key mechanism. It shows that a Mixer can be expressed as a wider MLP whose weights have a Kronecker-product structure.

That equivalent expression exposes several sparsity properties built into the architecture. For linear layers, it reveals an implicit sparse regularization effect and a connection to Monarch matrices, another sparse parameterization. These results provide a mathematical account of how the model's architecture constrains its effective connections.

For more general cases, experiments show quantitative similarities between Mixers and MLPs with unstructured sparse weights. The authors also find that Mixers can improve performance by increasing width and sparsity while keeping the number of connections fixed. This links an architectural explanation to a design principle: distributing a fixed connection budget across a wider, sparser model can be beneficial in the examined settings.
icml-2024-understanding-mlp-mixer-as-a-w.tldr: The paper explains MLP-Mixer as a wider, structured sparse MLP and connects its performance to architectural sparsity.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distances compare distributions through optimal transport, but computing many such comparisons becomes costly as a collection grows. Wasserstein Wormhole learns an embedding space where ordinary Euclidean distances approximate these transport distances. Its transformer-based autoencoder maps empirical distributions into that space and reconstructs distributions from their embeddings.

The authors extend multidimensional scaling theory to show that their training objective implies a bound on the error from embedding non-Euclidean distances. Empirically, distances in the learned space closely track Wasserstein distances. The method reports linear-time computation of OT distance approximations through this representation, providing a computationally convenient route to distribution comparison.

The decoder also makes the embedding useful for operations beyond measuring distance. Calculations performed in the latent space can map back to distributions, supporting Wasserstein barycenter estimation and transport interpolation. The contribution combines approximate transport geometry with a reversible learned representation, opening possibilities for scalable distribution analysis in areas such as computational geometry and single-cell biology.
icml-2024-wasserstein-wormhole-scalable-.tldr: Wasserstein Wormhole learns distribution embeddings whose Euclidean distances approximate optimal transport distances and whose decoder supports distribution-space operations.
